content: Noni juice has been associated with various therapeutic effects, including antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, antitumor, analgesic, hypotensive, anti-inflammatory, and immune-enhancing properties. It has also been shown to reduce total cholesterol and triglycerides. The root extract of noni juice may help alleviate chronic pain, painful inflammation, and swelling. Additionally, chewing noni leaves may aid in the management of diabetes by releasing and activating soluble dietary fiber, which slows the absorption of simple sugars in the gut. Extracts from the leaves of Morinda citrifolia have been used to treat parasitic infections, such as intestinal nematodes. When applied topically, noni juice may reduce inflammation and acne. Preliminary studies suggest potential antitumor effects, but reliable evidence is insufficient. Noni juice has been reported to increase serum potassium levels, which may interact with various medications. For example, it can amplify the potassium-raising effects of drugs such as amiloride, drospirenone, potassium supplements (e.g., potassium chloride, potassium citrate), spironolactone, and triamterene. These interactions necessitate close monitoring and caution due to the risk of hyperkalemia. Additionally, noni juice may interact with beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol), angiotensin receptor blockers (e.g., losartan, valsartan, irbesartan), and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen, diclofenac, and naproxen, all of which can also increase serum potassium. The clinical significance of these interactions is often unclear, but caution is advised. Conversely, noni juice may counteract the potassium-lowering effects of certain medications, such as loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) and thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide). The combined effect of these interactions is not well understood, and careful monitoring is recommended. Adverse effects associated with noni juice include acute hepatitis, liver toxicity, liver damage (potentially requiring liver transplantation), and hyperkalemia. Individuals with a history of hepatitis, liver disease, or advanced kidney disease should avoid noni juice. It may also have a laxative effect, causing diarrhea. To minimize risks, it is recommended to use the smallest effective quantity. There is no established pregnancy category for noni juice, and its safety during pregnancy and lactation is not well-documented. Controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking, and its use should be approached with caution.
